concepts.name: Rowlatt Act (1919): Legislative Origins and Legal Provisions
key_dimensions: Based on recommendations of Sedition Committee (1918) chaired by Justice S.A.T. Rowlatt — distinguish from Rowlatt himself being a British judge, not a politician
Key provisions: trial of seditious crimes without jury, detention without trial, restrictions on press — compare with Defence of India Act 1915
Officially called the Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act, 1919 — UPSC trap on official name vs popular name
Passed despite unanimous opposition of all Indian members of Imperial Legislative Council — significance of this political fact

concepts.name: Sedition Committee (Rowlatt Committee) 1918: Context and Recommendations
key_dimensions: Established to investigate 'revolutionary conspiracies' — specifically the Ghadr Movement and Bengal revolutionary activities post-WWI
Report recommended permanent extension of wartime emergency powers of Defence of India Act 1915 into peacetime law
Distinction: Rowlatt Committee was investigative, Rowlatt Act was legislative outcome — frequently confused
Context of post-WWI British anxiety about Indian nationalism and Bolshevik influence — why British considered it necessary

concepts.name: Gandhi's Response to Rowlatt Act: Satyagraha Sabha and Political Strategy
key_dimensions: Gandhi's first all-India political campaign — significance as transition from local (Champaran, Kheda, Ahmedabad) to national agitation
Formation of Satyagraha Sabha (February 1919) — Gandhi's instrument for organizing resistance, distinct from Congress organization
Hartal call of 6 April 1919 — significance of using economic shutdown as political tool, debate over its success
Gandhi's 'Himalayan miscalculation' — his own admission that he launched the movement before people were ready for non-violent discipline

concepts.name: Hartals and Violence of April 1919: From Ahmedabad to Delhi
key_dimensions: Violence in Ahmedabad (Gandhi's own base): burning of government buildings, killing of a police sergeant — tested Gandhi's non-violence commitment
Violence in Amritsar: killing of 5 Europeans including bank manager — directly precipitated martial law and General Dyer's actions
Gandhi's arrest near Delhi on 8 April 1919 and its consequences for crowd behavior — link between leadership removal and violence
UPSC trap: Violence preceded Jallianwala Bagh massacre, not the other way — sequence of events is frequently tested

concepts.name: Jallianwala Bagh Massacre (13 April 1919): Factual and Contextual Framework
key_dimensions: Date significance: Baisakhi festival — crowd was mix of pilgrims, local residents, and political protesters, not exclusively political gathering
General Reginald Dyer's order: 1,650 rounds fired without warning to disperse or evacuate, only stopped when ammunition exhausted
Official death toll vs. Indian National Congress estimate: 379 (official) vs. ~1,000+ (Congress/Hunter Committee minority) — this discrepancy is UPSC-relevant
Physical geography of Jallianwala Bagh: enclosed space with limited exits — Dyer's deliberate choice of sustained firing exploited this, central to his culpability

concepts.name: Martial Law in Punjab (1919): Scope and Atrocities
key_dimensions: Martial law declared in Amritsar and Lahore districts — distinguish which areas were covered vs. excluded
Specific humiliations ordered by Dyer: crawling order on the lane where Marcella Sherwood was attacked — symbolic of racial subjugation beyond the massacre
Flogging, detention without trial, forced saluting of Europeans — systematic nature of martial law excesses beyond Jallianwala Bagh alone
Lieutenant Governor Michael O'Dwyer's role: he approved Dyer's actions — UPSC trap of distinguishing Dyer (military commander) from O'Dwyer (civil authority)

concepts.name: Hunter Commission (Disorders Inquiry Committee, 1919-20): Composition and Findings
key_dimensions: Officially 'Disorders Inquiry Committee' — chaired by Lord William Hunter, hence Hunter Commission — know both names
Composition: mixed British and Indian members — Indian members included Jagat Narayan, C.H. Setalvad, Sultan Ahmed — their minority report is critical
Majority (British) report: censured Dyer but treated it as error of judgment, not criminal act — recommended no criminal prosecution
Minority (Indian) report: far more condemnatory, recommended stronger action — the divide reflects the political nature of the inquiry

concepts.name: General Dyer: Career Outcome and the 'Morning Post' Controversy
key_dimensions: Army Council's decision: Dyer was censured and relieved of command but faced no criminal prosecution — distinction between administrative and criminal accountability
House of Lords voted in Dyer's favor (129-86) vs. House of Commons censured him — reveals class/imperial divisions within British politics
Morning Post fundraiser: British public raised £26,000 for Dyer — 'Saviour of the Empire' narrative vs. Indian outrage
UPSC trap: Dyer was not court-martialed, not imprisoned — his punishment was effectively forced retirement, important factual distinction

concepts.name: Rabindranath Tagore's Renunciation of Knighthood: Significance
key_dimensions: Tagore renounced knighthood (conferred 1915) in protest against Jallianwala Bagh — letter to Viceroy Chelmsford is a primary source document
Symbolic importance: first major cultural figure to use honor-renunciation as political protest — established a template later used by others
Tagore's letter argued the 'enormity of the measures' made 'complacency' an 'insult to the humanity' — philosophical dimension beyond politics
Distinction: Tagore renounced knighthood, Gandhi renounced Kaisar-i-Hind medal (awarded for WWI ambulance work) — both as protest, UPSC may test which award each person renounced

concepts.name: Gandhi's Awards Renunciation and Suspension of Satyagraha (1919)
key_dimensions: Gandhi returned Kaisar-i-Hind gold medal, Zulu War medal, and Boer War medal — all three, not just one, important for completeness
Suspension of Rowlatt Satyagraha after violence: Gandhi's 'Himalayan miscalculation' statement — self-critical leadership and its political implications
Significance of suspension: established Gandhi's principle that satyagraha must be suspended if it turns violent — sets template for future movements
Contrast with later Non-Cooperation Movement (1922 Chauri Chaura): same principle applied — Jallianwala Bagh experience shaped Gandhi's later decisions

concepts.name: Congress Investigation Committee Report on Punjab (1920): Role of Gandhi and Nehru
key_dimensions: Congress conducted its own parallel inquiry — Gandhi drafted the report, establishing his narrative authority over the events
Motilal Nehru and Jawaharlal Nehru both participated — Jallianwala Bagh as formative event in Nehru family's radicalization
Congress report vs. Hunter Commission report: diametrically different conclusions — understanding both is essential for UPSC answer enrichment
The report's political use: Congress used it to demand accountability that Hunter Commission denied, building public opinion for Non-Cooperation

concepts.name: Jallianwala Bagh as Catalyst for Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22)
key_dimensions: Causal link: Punjab wrongs + Khilafat issue = twin justifications Gandhi cited for launching Non-Cooperation Movement in 1920
Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (1919) came simultaneously — UPSC trap: reforms and repression happened in same year, Indian leaders had to decide whether to cooperate or not
Transition from moderate constitutionalism to mass non-cooperation: Jallianwala Bagh discredited faith in British justice among moderates like Tilak and Surendranath Banerjee
Bal Gangadhar Tilak's response: called for swaraj as birthright — contrast with pre-Jallianwala moderate political approach

concepts.name: Michael O'Dwyer: Role, Justification, and Assassination
key_dimensions: Lieutenant Governor of Punjab: approved Dyer's actions and imposed harshest martial law measures — O'Dwyer was the civilian superior, often overlooked vs. Dyer
O'Dwyer's post-retirement book 'India As I Knew It' (1925) defended his actions — represents imperial viewpoint primary source
Assassination by Udham Singh in London (1940): killed O'Dwyer at Caxton Hall — UPSC trap: Udham Singh killed O'Dwyer, not Dyer (who died of natural causes in 1927)
Udham Singh's significance: represents radical nationalist response to Jallianwala Bagh two decades later, connects 1919 to 1940 revolutionary nationalism

concepts.name: Udham Singh (Ram Mohammad Singh Azad): Revolutionary Nationalist Response
key_dimensions: Claimed to have been present at Jallianwala Bagh as a child — personal witness to massacre, motivational basis for assassination
Alias 'Ram Mohammad Singh Azad' — representing Hindu-Muslim-Sikh unity, deliberate composite identity choice
Tried and hanged in Britain (1940) — not in India — jurisdiction and legal proceedings location is a factual trap
Distinction from Bhagat Singh's legacy: both are Punjab revolutionaries, both hanged, but different eras, methods, and targets — UPSC frequently tests comparisons

concepts.name: Jallianwala Bagh National Memorial: Post-Independence Commemoration
key_dimensions: Jallianwala Bagh National Memorial Act, 1951 — established Trust to maintain the site, composition of Trust includes PM, Congress President, Punjab CM
Congress President's inclusion in Trust: a statutory provision — UPSC trap as this is unusual for a government trust to include a party official
2019 Amendment to the Act: removed Congress President from Trust, replaced with Leader of Opposition or largest opposition party leader — controversial amendment
Centenary commemoration (2019) and British apology debate: UK expressed 'deep regret' but stopped short of formal apology — contemporary relevance for UPSC

concepts.name: Rowlatt Act vs. Defence of India Act (1915): Comparative Analysis
key_dimensions: Defence of India Act 1915: temporary wartime measure, expired after WWI — Rowlatt Act was attempt to make similar powers permanent in peacetime
Key distinction: wartime emergency justification vs. peacetime preventive detention — the latter was constitutionally and morally more contestable
Both allowed detention without trial, but Rowlatt Act also restricted jury trials for sedition — the jury provision was particularly objectionable to legal professionals
Legacy: Rowlatt Act was never actually used against any individual — its significance was symbolic and political, not operational — important UPSC trap

concepts.name: Indian Members' Opposition in Imperial Legislative Council: Constitutional Significance
key_dimensions: All 22 Indian members voted against the Rowlatt Act — unanimous opposition across political spectrum (moderates, nationalists, Muslims, Hindus)
Notable opponents: Muhammad Ali Jinnah resigned from Imperial Legislative Council in protest — significance for Jinnah's early nationalist credentials
Mazhar-ul-Haq, Madan Mohan Malaviya also opposed — shows cross-communal unity before Khilafat period
Institutional lesson: nominated Indian members could be overridden by official majority — demonstrated futility of constitutional methods, feeding non-cooperation rationale

concepts.name: Khilafat-Rowlatt Act Nexus: Communal Unity in 1919-20
key_dimensions: Jallianwala Bagh and Rowlatt Act protests saw Hindu-Muslim joint participation — contrast with later communal tensions
Gandhi's strategic decision to support Khilafat cause simultaneously with Punjab grievances: twin planks of Non-Cooperation
UPSC trap: Khilafat Movement was about Ottoman Caliphate, not directly related to Rowlatt Act, but Gandhi linked them tactically — understand the distinction and the linkage
Both issues were resolved/deflated by external events (Hunter Report inadequacy + abolition of Caliphate by Ataturk 1924) — explaining decline of the combined movement

concepts.name: Role of Press and Censorship in Rowlatt Act Period
key_dimensions: Rowlatt Act included press restriction provisions — continuation of wartime censorship into peacetime
Tribune (Lahore) and other Punjab papers: suppression of massacre news, delayed public awareness outside Punjab
Gandhi's Young India and Navajivan newspapers used to build nationalist narrative — started in 1919, directly linked to post-Rowlatt political communication strategy
Contrast: how news of Jallianwala Bagh reached British Parliament — Sir Chettur Sankaran Nair's role and his book 'Gandhi and Anarchy' (1932) as a critical counter-narrative

concepts.name: Jallianwala Bagh in Comparative Colonial Context: Global and Historiographical Dimensions
key_dimensions: Comparison with Amritsar massacre vs. other colonial repression events: what made Jallianwala Bagh uniquely significant in anti-colonial discourse
Churchill's denunciation in Parliament: called it 'monstrous' — UPSC may use Churchill quote to test whether it was supportive or critical
Historiographical debate: Nick Lloyd's 'The Amritsar Massacre' (2011) vs. Kim Wagner's 'Amritsar 1919' (2019) — different interpretations of Dyer's intent and crowd composition
Contemporary relevance: 2019 British 'deep regret' vs. demand for formal apology — connects historical event to current India-UK relations, relevant for GS-2
